PRE-MARKET, Election Day (Nov 3 US midterms per mpamag). The tech unwind is still the main story. In the last cash session the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.07% (-272.64) to 25164.36 and the S&P 500 fell 0.51% to 7541.4, while the Dow rose 0.41%. That gap reflects rotation inside the market, not broad selling: Info Tech was -2.66% and Energy -3.97%, against Cons Discr +2.25%, Materials +1.83%, Financials +1.76% and Staples +1.75%. Futures are mixed this morning. ES is -0.06%, NQ +0.35% and Dow futures -0.59%, ahead of AMD's results after the close. Yields are rising everywhere. The US 10Y is at 4.9373% (+2.48bp), the 30Y at 5.3071%, Gilts +5.5bp at 5.247% and Bunds +3.6bp, and that keeps the pressure on long-duration growth stocks. Europe is lower (FTSE -0.64%, SX5E -0.34%), copper is -2.68%, and VIX is at 21.27. In credit, the computed HY contagion panel deserves attention. The Caa–B gap is 780bp, against a 5-year average near 417bp. That puts it at the 99.5th percentile of the past five years, it has widened +236bp over 3 months, and Caa spreads are the widest since April 2020. The stress is now edging up the quality ladder. Single-B OAS widened +36bp over the past month to 333bp and Ba widened +20bp to 204bp. The 63-day Caa/B correlation has risen to 0.65 from 0.41 three months ago, though it is still below its 5-year median of 0.69. Headline IG (0.92%, 18th percentile) and HY (3.39%) are still historically tight, so the stress has not reached investment grade in any meaningful way. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. CoreWeave 5Y CDS is at 1153.5bp, 41bp below its 1,194.5bp record, and Nvidia CDS eased 1.79bp. On that evidence the market is still giving some credit to Nvidia's backstop, but the CoreWeave notes made new price lows. The computed tech-phase model still places the basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), 19 days after the peak. One signpost has now triggered: 57.1% of basket names are more than 20% off their highs, against a 50% line. SOX is 29.43% below its 52-week high, just 0.57pp short of its -30% signpost. The model's 6-month Phase 2/3 odds fell 5.3pp versus Oct 30. It puts the chance of reaching Phase 2 or worse within 12 months at 56.3%; these are model estimates, not certainties. Sentiment is defensive but orderly.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 451.97 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is trading at 451.97 cents/gal, and nearly every gauge on it is at a historical extreme. The outright price sits at the 99.5th percentile, the crack spread is at a z-score of 4.83, and the curve is in steep backwardation: the front month is 96.72 cents/gal over the 12th month and 178.56 over the 36th. That points to an acute shortage of prompt barrels and very rich refining margins, not a broad repricing of the whole curve. Past episodes like this have tended to unwind from the front of the curve, so all five cards lean SELL. The stops are very wide, though, which shows how violent squeezes at these extremes can be.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.66 vol points (41th percentile of the 59 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 100.4 (72th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 84bp (steeper by 4bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 33 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 55/100 — Sticky but not re-accelerating at the core; headline pressure comes from energy. The trimmed and median measures are flat around 2.3–2.8%. Median CPI (2.61%) is edging lower, while flexible CPI (6.12%, rising, 82nd percentile) carries the oil shock. Breadth is uncomfortable. The Dallas distribution shows 52.6% of the PCE basket above 3% (16.6% above 10%, 10.2% at 5–10%, 25.8% at 3–5%), and only 25.6% is falling. Core PCE at 3.12% is still well above target. Read: the core-trend percentiles (see computed sub-score) sit in the middle of the historical range, so persistence is moderate and not spiralling. Wages (AHE 3.0%) are not driving it. Oil is the main upside risk, and the Fed has little room to ease.

🫧Tech Bubble Peak Again?vs March 2000
BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
8 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 7 beyond 2000 — 58/100
Today is not the March 2000 peak on equity froth, but late-cycle conditions are at or past 2000 levels. Equity froth is well short: Nasdaq trailing P/E is 39.2x, only 15% of the way to the 175x 2000 peak. Price stretch has collapsed to 1% (Nasdaq 0.4% above its 200DMA) and SOX P/E is at 39%. The late-cycle catalyst and regime gauges look different. IG tightness reads 123%, Baa–10Y tightness 155%, NFCI looseness 152%, VIX complacency 126% and commodities-vs-equities 200%, meaning credit and financial conditions are as loose as or looser than in 2000, while the curve (68%) and PMIs (1–10%) are not yet rolling over. The computed phase model puts the tech basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), with a basket drawdown of -17.9% against -22.67% for the 2000 basket on the same day. Model odds (estimates, not certainties): 56.5% still in Phase 1 at 6 months; 56.3% chance of ever reaching Phase 2+ within 12 months; Phase 4 (trough/healing) is the modal state at 24 months (50.3%). The breadth signpost has triggered and SOX is 0.57pp from its -30% line. Overall this is a mid-cycle valuation de-rating inside loose credit conditions, not a 2000-style blow-off.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The froth gauges have reset hard. The Nasdaq is down about 10% from its 52-week high, semis are down about 29%, and the AI-infrastructure names are down 45–70% (CoreWeave -63.65%, IREN -71.18%). Valuations are still very high by long history. Our analyst estimates put Shiller CAPE near 40x (Finnovate's October monthly reading was 41.07 before the recent drop), top-10 concentration near 39% (S&P DJI via Finnovate 37.8% at end-August; another guide cites 40.6%) and market cap/GDP above 200%. Those are close to 2000 extremes on breadth of valuation, if not on Nasdaq P/E. What differs from 2000 is that the stress is showing up in credit before the economy: CCC spreads are at 5-year extremes and neocloud CDS are near records while IG is tight. In the model's terms, the P1→P2 transition is a credit event, and the signposts to watch are HY above 4.20%, Baa–10Y above 195bp and CoreWeave CDS above 1,194.5bp. Positioning is not euphoric: AAII bull–bear is -3.6pp and put/call is 0.67, so the sentiment fuel that drove 2000 is missing. The tilt the model associates with this phase mix is gold, Treasury duration and IG over mega-cap growth and EM.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Hold at 3.50–3.75% at the next meeting (inference). The Fed has kept rates there at every reported Warsh-era meeting. The Oct 27–28 decision was not verified in this run's searches. With core PCE at 3.12%, the 10Y at 4.94% and claims at 194k, there is no case for a cut, and Warsh has signalled independence on inflation.

~1 YEAR

Inference (analyst estimate): policy rate roughly unchanged to modestly lower over 12 months. Warsh likely puts balance-sheet reduction and an institutional/communications overhaul ahead of rate moves. The committee is hawkish (9 of 19 saw a 2026 hike in June), but Warsh declined to submit a dot, which suggests he will resist a hike unless core inflation re-accelerates. A credit-led tech unwind (the Phase 2 path) would be the trigger for cuts.

Verified facts: Kevin Warsh was sworn in as the 17th Fed chair on May 22, 2026. His first FOMC (June) left the funds rate at 3.50–3.75% unanimously. The June projections showed 9 of 19 participants expecting a hike by end-2026, and Warsh did not submit a dot. He began his term with a sweeping review of the Fed. The next meeting was listed as Oct 27–28, just before the Nov 3 midterms; its outcome is not verified here. Inference (flagged): his long-standing on-record views favour a smaller balance sheet, less forward guidance and less data-point dependence. Together with sticky core PCE and a rising long end, that points to a patient hold. The main 1-year risk is a fight between a hawkish committee and a chair who leans toward rebuilding credibility rather than hiking. Not re-verified in this run.
